never: Never write flat, uniformly medium-length sentences—Poe's rhythm lives in the violent contrast between long periodic swells and abrupt short shocks.
Never keep an even, modern, businesslike register; avoid plain contemporary diction where an antique, Latinate, sonorous word (sepulchral, ineffable, tenebrous) would carry more weight.
Never deliver the horror as a single sudden jolt; dread must arrive by gradual, perceptible degrees.
Never stay cool and detached—the narrator's nerves, dread, and obsession must color every clause.
Never leave the supernatural vague and unmeasured; refusing exact detail (fathoms, angles, the minute on a watch) drains Poe of his uncanny authority.
Never narrate from a calm, omniscient distance; Poe testifies in the first person from inside the disturbed mind.
Never resolve cleanly or reassure the reader; leave the tale charged with terror, mystery, or a thing 'which should not be told.'
Never suppress the dash and the italic—they are the load-bearing punctuation of suspension and emphasis.
always: Always vary pacing sharply: long, clause-stacked periodic sentences broken by curt declaratives ('Here died my mother. Herein was I born.').
Always deploy the dash to suspend, interrupt, and re-aim a thought mid-breath.
Always use rhetorical repetition as incantation—echo a word or clause until it turns hypnotic ('down, down, down'; 'now—now').
Always ground the impossible in clinical, exact measurement to make it feel inevitable.
Always pile sensory detail toward suffocation—sound on sound, gloom on gloom.
Always write the body in extremity, reporting physical sensation with unblinking precision.
Always italicize the single word that carries the horror or the turn.
Always address the reader directly, anticipating and disarming his disbelief.
